lead: One force can be split into components. Varignon's theorem says the turning effect of the whole force about a point equals the sum of the turning effects of its parts about that same point. This matters because the perpendicular distance to an inclined force is awkward to measure, while components lying along and across a beam have distances you can read straight off a drawing. Everyone who analyses a crane jib, a bracket or a leaning ladder uses this shortcut to turn one difficult force into two easy ones.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.2 for M = Fd with its sign convention, and Unit 1, resolution and composition of forces, for Fx = F cos θ and Fy = F sin θ.

sections.h3: The statement, and why it exists

blocks.text: A force F acts at point A of a rigid body. Replace it by any number of components F₁, F₂, …, Fₙ that also act at A and whose vector sum is F. Varignon's theorem states that the moment of F about a point O equals the sum of the moments of the components about the same point O:

blocks.where: M<sub>O</sub> is the moment of the force about O (N·m); F<sub>i</sub> are the component magnitudes (N); d<sub>i</sub> are the perpendicular distances from O to each component's line of action (m), with d<sub>i</sub> ≥ 0; s<sub>i</sub> = +1 for an anticlockwise moment and s<sub>i</sub> = −1 for a clockwise moment.

blocks.text: The theorem exists because of one practical difficulty. For a force at 30° to the horizontal, finding the perpendicular distance from O to its line of action needs geometry: extend the line, drop a perpendicular, solve a triangle. For its horizontal and vertical components, the perpendicular distances are simply a vertical and a horizontal distance on your sketch. So you trade one hard distance for two easy ones.

items: Inclined forces: split into horizontal and vertical, then add two moments instead of hunting one perpendicular distance.
One force into two convenient ones: a force on a ladder can be split along the ladder and across it, matching the geometry you already have.
Chain of parts: the same idea applies to a force already given as components, or to three components in space — add all the moments.
Moment about an axis: take moments of the components about the axis instead of the axis distance of the whole force. See Chapter 2.2.

blocks.text: Place O at the origin of x–y axes. The point of application A has coordinates (x, y) in metres, and the force has components F<sub>x</sub> and F<sub>y</sub> in newtons, both acting at A.

Only the vertical component has a horizontal lever arm: F<sub>y</sub> acts on a vertical line through A, whose perpendicular distance from O is x. Its moment is about the z-axis through O (perpendicular to the plane), and it is anticlockwise, so the term is +x F<sub>y</sub>. Only the horizontal component has a vertical lever arm: F<sub>x</sub> acts on a horizontal line at height y, whose perpendicular distance from O is y. Its moment is also about the z-axis through O and is clockwise, so the term is −y F<sub>x</sub>.

blocks.where: x, y are the coordinates of the point of application A (m); F<sub>x</sub>, F<sub>y</sub> are the force components at A (N); M_O is the moment about O (N·m), anticlockwise positive.

blocks.text: Every extra force or component you add at A contributes one more term x F<sub>y</sub> − y F<sub>x</sub> with the same x and y, and the terms simply add. That is the theorem for any number of components. The perpendicular distance is not needed at all.

sections.h3: When it holds and when it fails

blocks.text: The theorem is about one force and its own parts, so the parts must act at the same point of application A as the original force. Two relaxations are allowed, and one is not.

items: Point O may be anywhere: on the body, off the body, on the line of action (then M_O = 0).
A component may be slid along its own line of action, because a force can be moved along its line of action without changing its moment — Chapter 2.1.
A component may not be moved to a different, parallel line. Its perpendicular distance from O changes, so its moment changes, and the sum no longer equals M_O.
A force already given as two components is not a special case: the theorem is being used in reverse.

blocks.text: Sign discipline is where marks are lost. Fix one sense as positive before you start, write each term with its sign, and keep the sign in the arithmetic. A clockwise component moment does not disappear; it subtracts.

figure.caption: The moment of the 50 N force splits into the moment of its vertical component, 75 N·m anticlockwise, and the moment of its horizontal component, −43.3 N·m. The two terms add to the total 31.7 N·m.

spec.aria: The total moment M_O of 31.7 N·m splits into a vertical-component moment of 75 N·m and a horizontal-component moment of minus 43.3 N·m, which add up to it.

examples.question: A force of 50 N acts at point A of a rigid body. Point A is 3 m to the right of and 1 m above point O. The force lies in the plane of the paper and points up and to the right at 30° to the horizontal. Using Varignon's theorem, find (a) the moment of the force about O, and (b) the perpendicular distance from O to its line of action.
steps: Resolve the force at A. F_x = 50 cos 30° = 43.3 N to the right; F_y = 50 sin 30° = 25 N upwards. Both act at A.
Take anticlockwise as positive. F_y acts on a vertical line 3 m from O (x = 3 m) and turns anticlockwise: moment = +3 × 25 = +75 N·m.
F_x acts on a horizontal line 1 m above O (y = 1 m) and turns clockwise: moment = −1 × 43.3 = −43.3 N·m.
Add the moments: M_O = x F_y − y F_x = 75 − 43.3 = 31.7 N·m, positive, so anticlockwise.
Perpendicular distance: for a single force M_O = F d, so d = M_O / F = 31.7 / 50 = 0.634 m.

The 50 N force is steeper than OA (30° against about 18.4°), so its line of action passes below O, with the perpendicular foot down and to the right. A force along that line pointing up and right turns the body anticlockwise about O; the positive sign agrees.
examples.answer: The moment about O is 31.7 N·m anticlockwise, and the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action is 0.634 m.
examples.check:
import math
F = 50.0
theta = math.radians(30)
x = 3.0
y = 1.0
Fx = F * math.cos(theta)
Fy = F * math.sin(theta)
M = x * Fy - y * Fx
d = M / F
print(round(Fx, 1))
print(round(Fy, 1))
print(round(M, 1))
print(round(d, 3))

examples.question: A 60 N force acts at a point 2 m to the left of O and 4 m above O, pointing down and to the right at 40° below the horizontal. Find its moment about O.
steps: Coordinates of A: x = −2 m, y = +4 m.
Components: F_x = 60 cos 40° = 46.0 N to the right; F_y = 60 sin 40° = 38.6 N downwards, so F_y = −38.6 N.
Sign for F_x: rightward, so positive. Sign for F_y: downward, so negative.
examples.answer: The moment about O is 106.8 N·m clockwise.
examples.check:
import math
F = 60.0
t = math.radians(40)
x = -2.0
y = 4.0
Fx = F*math.cos(t)
Fy = -F*math.sin(t)
print(round(Fx, 1))
print(round(Fy, 1))
print(round(x*Fy - y*Fx, 1))

traps: Using the slant distance OA instead of the perpendicular distance to the line of action: 3 m and 1 m fix the point, not the lever arm.
Dropping the sign of one component's moment: the two terms often oppose, and 75 + 43.3 instead of 75 − 43.3 gives a wrong total and a wrong sense.
Mixing units: distances in mm with forces in kN must be converted before adding moments, and the answer carries N·m or kN·m, never N.
Placing a component on a parallel line instead of at the same point of application, which silently changes its moment.
Writing the clockwise term first and then calling the anticlockwise result negative out of habit; fix the positive sense at the start and state it in the answer.

quiz.q: State Varignon's theorem for a force and its components.
quiz.a: The moment of a force about a point equals the algebraic sum of the moments of its components about the same point, all components acting at the same point of application as the force.

quiz.q: Why does the theorem make an inclined force easier to handle than one perpendicular distance calculation?
quiz.a: The perpendicular distance to an inclined line of action needs construction. The horizontal and vertical components have lever arms equal to the vertical and horizontal distances already marked on the sketch, so two simple products replace one hard geometry step.

quiz.q: A 100 N force acts at a point 4 m to the right of and 2 m above O, pointing up and to the right at 45° to the horizontal. Find its moment about O.
An 80 N horizontal force acts at a point 4 m directly above O and points to the right. Find its moment about O using the theorem.
quiz.a: F_x = 80 N, F_y = 0. M_O = 0×0 − 4×80 = −320 N·m, that is 320 N·m clockwise.

quiz.q: A student slides one component of a force 1 m sideways, parallel to itself, and still adds its moment to the others. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: The component's perpendicular distance from O changes, so its moment changes. The sum no longer equals the moment of the original force. Sliding along the component's own line of action is allowed; sliding to a parallel line is not.

quiz.q: A force passes through O. What does Varignon's theorem say about the moments of its components, and why is that consistent?
quiz.a: M_O = 0, so the component moments must cancel in the algebraic sum. Each component line still has some perpendicular distance from O, but the two terms are equal and opposite, giving zero net turning.

quiz.q: Does Varignon's theorem depend on the choice of point O?
quiz.a: No. The identity holds for every point O, but the numerical value of M_O changes with O; only for a couple is the moment the same about all points. See Chapter 2.4.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same add-the-parts idea becomes the vector cross product M = r × F, which is how software computes moments in 3D assemblies. In finite element codes, loads on a surface are integrated into nodal forces and moments using exactly this decomposition. Robotics uses it to convert a force at the tool tip into joint torques through the Jacobian. Search for "moment of a force vector product" and "equivalent force-couple system in 3D" to go further.
